title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
content: Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. A No 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world". Speaking on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford. He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out." Rubio said the US still has full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities have been very cooperative since the incident. US Vice President JD Vance later said the bombers were moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington feels Iran is doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people". RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police. Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail. Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire. The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts. Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials. The newspaper wrote that the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours. Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, called the US' decision "prudent". He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced anymore, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it from all sorts of threats." It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year . But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will see the US lose a foothold for the country outside continental Europe. Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called the US' decision to withdraw its bombers "deeply concerning" and called for the government to set out a plan to ensure the country's military bases are "fit for purpose". Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. Residents living close to RAF Fairford told the BBC of their relief at the departure of bombers from the airbase, with one local saying she was "thrilled," citing the noise and feeling "increasingly vulnerable" in recent weeks. Another villager, who said he has seen bombs being loaded aboard aircraft from his back garden, said he knew something was happening when he saw planes leaving "one, after another, after another" on Sunday. The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions. It labelled Anthropic a "supply chain risk" in February after the firm refused to remove safety guardrails from its tools. The woman alleges she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house at the university two years ago. A homecoming celebration turned into a scene of deadly violence, as dozens of shots were fired into a crowd. No reason has been given for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident last week when police were alerted to "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
content: A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country. The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch. "The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby. Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days. There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury. The AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand. However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade. "He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying. When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified. "Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media. A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened". The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said. Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school. "At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media. "Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred." The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on. "In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment." According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began. Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country. High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands. More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according to AFP, with around 85% of them minors. The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike. Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected. Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted. But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets. Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest. In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced. Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October.
